newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Nemtsov visits Russia's crisis-hit Far East.
newsitem.headline: Nemtsov visits Russia's crisis-hit Far East.

text.p: First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, on a whirlwind trip to Russia's troubled Far East, signalled on Wednesday that Moscow might sack the region's governor over his handling of an energy crisis.

Nemtsov said he would brief President Boris Yeltsin on the findings of a government commission investigating power cuts in Primorsky Krai region that have pitted populist governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko against the Kremlin's liberal reformers.
"Everything that is happening in Primorksy Krai I shall be reporting to the president," Nemtsov told reporters in the regional capital Vladivostok.

Yeltsin, exasperated by the failure of local politicians to end the energy crisis, undercut Nazdratenko's authority last week by awarding sweeping powers to his new personal representative in the region, Viktor Kondratov.

Kondratov, head of the regional branch of the Federal Security Service, said then that, in addition to the energy crisis, organised crime and high-level corruption in Primorsky Krai had reached dangerous proportions and the local administration showed little ability to tackle them.
Nemtsov defended the appointment of Kondratov and said Yeltsin had the right to suspend Nazdratenko from office if he saw fit after studying the commission's findings.
"If there is order in Primorsky Krai there will be no personnel changes. But if things remain the same the country's leadership will take the necessary measures," he said.
He made clear this would probably mean early elections in the strategically-important region, which lies seven time zones and 7,000 km (4,500 miles) away from Moscow.
Nemtsov, who stopped in Vladivostok on his way back to Moscow after a visit to Japan, said that higher energy tariffs -- long resisted by Nazdratenko -- were inevitable to end the power cuts.
But he promised more federal support for the local economy, including the payment of all debts owed by Moscow and a push for cheaper rail freight charges to increase trade.
The federal government would react firmly to any "provocative" appeals by local politicians to citizens not to pay the higher energy tariffs, Nemtsov said.
Nazdratenko, a former mining engineer who is known to dislike the liberals now running Russia's economy, has said energy price rises would cripple industry.
In Moscow, the other first deputy prime minister, Anatoly Chubais, joined the offensive against Nazdratenko, saying he bore the main responsibility for the energy crisis.
"We have had enough of having to carry the blame for the fantastic unprofessionalism and helplessness of local leaders," said Chubais, clearly referring to Nazdratenko.

But removing Nazdratenko, a democratically-elected leader, would be politically and constitutionally awkward for Yeltsin. Nazdratenko, long adept at shifting the blame for his region's problems onto Moscow, might well win any early election.
"The struggle in and for the Primorye region is only just beginning," said the Obschaya Gazeta weekly.
Nazdratenko's colleagues in Russia's upper house Federation Council urged the government to respect the constitution and not to try removing him forcefully from office, Interfax news agency said.
The upper house is composed of regional governors and the presidents of local parliaments.
